paper_title: PAR: Progress-Aligned Recurrence for Length Generalization in State Tracking

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Looped language models can run more iterations at test time, but additional iterations need not help them solve longer problems. For sequential state tracking, final-answer supervision does not specify how far each iteration should advance, and repeated updates can change the scale of the recurrent state. We introduce \textbf{Progress-Aligned Recurrence (PAR)}, which trains the prediction at iteration $k$ to match the state after the first $k$ operations and rescales recurrent states to their first-iteration norms. On swap-$S_5$, a Qwen2.5-0.5B model trained on at most 32 moves achieves 95.5\% mean full-state accuracy at 512 moves, or $16\times$ the training length, compared with 55.7\% reported for RLT and 0.8\% for explicit chain of thought on the same backbone. Controlled $S_5$ ablations show that removing norm anchoring reduces the extrapolation factor from $16\times$ to below $2.2\times$, and replacing progress-aligned targets with final-answer supervision reduces it to at most $8\times$. A learned completion readout selects when to answer without a supplied stopping depth. When intermediate labels are unavailable, prefix self-distillation induces the correspondence from shorter problem prefixes using only final answers. The gains apply across sequential state-tracking tasks, establishing the task structure required for depth extrapolation. These findings support training intermediate predictions and state scale together to make additional recurrent depth useful for longer problems.

sections.content: Looped language models can run more iterations at test time, but additional iterations need not help them solve longer problems. For sequential state tracking, final-answer supervision does not specify how far each iteration should advance, and repeated updates can change the scale of the recurrent state. We introduce Progress-Aligned Recurrence (PAR), which trains the prediction at iteration 𝑘 to match the state after the first 𝑘 operations and rescales recurrent states to their first-iteration norms. On swap-𝑆5, Qwen2.5-0.5B model trained on at most 32 moves achieves 95.5% mean full-state accuracy at 512 moves, or 16 the training length, compared with 55.7% reported for RLT and 0.8% for explicit chain of thought on the same backbone. When intermediate labels are unavailable, prefix self-distillation induces the correspondence from shorter problem prefixes using only final answers. Keywords: looped language models, length generalization, state tracking, recurrent depth, latent reasoning

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Length generalisation asks whether model trained on short problems can solve longer instances of the same task [1, 7]. Sequential state tracking provides controlled setting for studying this question: each operation updates state used by later operations [19]. rule-table chain, for example, uses each retrieved value to select the next lookup, while object tracking updates the locations of objects after each move [28, 29]. In these tasks, the rules remain unchanged as the sequence grows; the model must apply them correctly over more steps. Throughout this paper, length refers to the number of task operations. Looped language models offer way to make computational depth grow with this length. They repeatedly apply shared transformer block to hidden states, allowing additional computation without generating text description of each step [5, 9], and can be added to pretrained language models [20]. Iterations have thus been proposed as scaling axis alongside parameters, improving test-time reasoning *Equal Contributions. [9] and following predictable training trends [22]. On longer problems, however, neither axis helps by itself: on 𝑆5 trained with at most 16 operations, an untied model with four times the core depth and recurrent model run with more iterations both extrapolate less than 2, and fixed-depth Qwen2.5 models from 1.5B to 7B stay near chance at 16 (5.1, 5.2). Prior work demonstrates length generalisation by tying the loop count to task length [7], and shows that intermediatestate supervision can teach pretrained model to perform successive rule lookups [28]. We build on these results to study how to sustain accurate execution over much longer operation sequences. central training choice is what to ask each intermediate loop to predict. final-answer target does not specify the state after only some operations. On graph reachability, Chen [4] finds that asking for the final answer at every loop encourages early predictions and weakens extrapolation. Intermediate-state targets define progress more directly, but their effectiveness also depends on the recurrence itself. In our state-tracking experiments, such targets without norm anchoring lose accuracy beyond short extrapolation distances ANT INTERNATIONAL RESEARCH PAR: Progress-Aligned Recurrence for Length Generalization (6.1). We therefore study progress-aligned supervision together with control of the scale of states passed between loops. We introduce Progress-Aligned Recurrence (PAR) for pretrained language models. At supervised iteration 𝑘, the prediction is trained to match the state after the first 𝑘 operations (Figure 1a). This depthlength correspondence assigns successive task stages to successive loop outputs: on rule-table chain, for instance, iteration 𝑘 predicts the value reached after 𝑘 lookups. To control state scale, PAR rescales each tokens recurrent state to its first-iteration root-meansquare norm. The targets specify the intended progress, while norm anchoring fixes state magnitude as the shared block is reused. The correspondence also guides when to read the answer and how to obtain intermediate targets. correct answer can deteriorate if the model continues looping after completion (5.3). We train the existing output layer to predict whether execution is complete, and use short confirmation window to select the answer without supplied stopping depth. When intermediate labels are unavailable, we use prefixes that are themselves valid shorter problems. Our prefix selfdistillation uses predictions on such prefixes as targets for the corresponding iterations on the full input, learning from final-answer labels alone. Our contributions are: We formulate length generalization in looped models as establishing depthlength correspondence, identifying state drift and unaligned loop targets as twin failure modes and proposing Progress-Aligned Recurrence (PAR) to couple progress supervision with RMS norm anchoring. We extend PAR with parameter-free learned halting rule to stop inference autonomously and prefix self-distillation to induce the correspondence without intermediate step labels. We demonstrate 16 extrapolation on swap-𝑆5 (95.5% fullstate accuracy vs. 55.7% for RLT and 0.8% for explicit CoT), show consistent benefits across backbones up to 7B, and isolate the necessity of both components through controlled ablations.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers. Weightsharing across depth originated in Universal Transformers [5], and recurrence can extend computation to harder instances [3, 27]. In language models, recurrent depth has been trained from scratch [9] or retrofitted into pretrained models [20]. Looped architectures can simulate chain of thought [25], exhibit stable scaling behavior [22], share representations across depths [15], and relate to implicit models [26], though depth is frequently underutilized [33]. We address this by defining what each iteration computes. Length extrapolation and halting. Prior work links loop count to input length [7] or explicit reasoning steps [8]. From-scratch looped models examine stochastic stopping [16], mechanistic limits [18], stability conditions [17], and fastslow recurrence [30]; among them, RLT [41] achieves strong swap-𝑆5 performance via token-level feedback. In retrofitted models, per-loop supervision yields modest extrapolation [28], whereas step-wise final-answer supervision impairs compositional generalization [4]. For terminating recurrence, adaptive computation time [10] and PonderNet [2] train halting probabilities with dedicated modules and ponder penalties. Under our correspondence, the existing output head detects completion directly, requiring neither extra parameters nor ponder losses. Latent reasoning and self-supervision. Coconut [12] and stepwise internalization [6] internalize reasoning along the sequence dimension using chain-of-thought data. In contrast, we compute along depth, using intermediate labels or prefix self-distillation inspired by mean-teacher consistency [31], in the spirit of work that derives training signals from models own outputs, interactions, or environments [13, 32, 34, 35, 39, 42]. While randomized positional encodings improve sequence generalization [24], our positional stretch stabilizes the recurrent step map when scaling to longer contexts without step labels.

sections.title: 3 Depth–Length Correspondence
sections.content: Figure 2 outlines the PAR framework. We realize the depth length correspondence by combining retrofitted recurrence with RMS norm anchoring to maintain stationary step map (3.1, 3.3), supervising each loop with progress-aligned targets (3.2), reading completion autonomously via learned halting (3.4), and extending the supervision to label-free settings through prefix self-distillation (3.5).

sections.title: 3.1 A retrofitted looped language model
sections.content: Following McLeish et al. [20], we split the 24 layers of Qwen2.5-0.5B [14] into prelude 𝑃 (layers 18), weighttied core 𝐶 (layers 916) and coda 𝑄 (layers 1724), as shown in Figure 2a. With static input features 𝑒 = 𝑃(𝑥) and 𝑠0 = 𝑒, the adapter 𝑊 projects the concatenated representations into the core, iterating 𝑠𝑘 = 𝐶 (𝑊 [𝑒; 𝑠𝑘1]) , 𝑘 = 1, . . . , 𝑅, (1) and reads an answer 𝑦𝑘 = 𝑄(𝑠𝑘) from any iteration. The adapter 𝑊 Rℎ2ℎ is initialised to [0 𝐼], so with 𝑅 = 1 the retrofitted model initially computes the same function as its parent. All weights are trained, gradients flow through the last 8 iterations, and answers are read with classification head over the candidate answer tokens at the query position.

sections.title: 3.3 Keeping the step map stationary
sections.content: Extrapolation applies the step map hundreds of times, far beyond the training depths, so anything that drifts with 𝑘 or with absolute position eventually changes what the map computes. We remove two such drifts. State-norm anchoring rescales every tokens state to the RMS norm of its first-iteration state after each iteration (Figure 2a), 𝑠𝑘 𝑠𝑘 rms(𝑠1)/rms(𝑠𝑘), with stop-gradient on the reference; 𝑅 = 1 is unchanged. Positional stretch addresses long prompts, in which the query lies far from early moves: during short fine-tuning stage we multiply position indices by 𝑠 𝑈 [1, 𝑠max], ramping 𝑠max from 1 to 8 [cf. 24], and test with ordinary positions. Label-supervised PAR reaches 16 without the stretch; the label-free variant did not reach 16 until fine-tuned with it (6.3).

sections.title: 3.4 Reading completion: learned halting
sections.content: Under the correspondence, whether the computation has finished is property of the iteration index and the problem, so it can be supervised. As illustrated in Figure 2d, the coda read-out that produces the answer is also trained to put probability on the token Yes when 𝑐𝑘 𝑑 and on No otherwise, using class-balanced cross-entropy with weight 0.5 on every supervised iteration plus one earlier iteration as an extra negative. No parameters are added, and training never runs an iteration beyond 𝑑. At test time we select the first answer iteration 𝑅 with 𝑃(Yes) > 𝜏 such that at least 𝑘 of the iterations 𝑅, . . . , 𝑅 + 𝑚 1 also exceed 𝜏. After checking this confirmation window, we return the prediction made at 𝑅. We use 𝜏 = 0.5, 𝑘 = 6, 𝑚 = 8; 6.2 explains how this rule was chosen.

sections.title: 3.5 Correspondence without step labels: prefix self-
sections.content: distillation Intermediate answers 𝑧 𝑗 come for free from synthetic generator but not from most real data. The correspondence supplies them anyway: the first 𝑗 steps of problem form shorter problem whose answer is 𝑧 𝑗 , and shorter problems are the ones model learns first. As shown in Figure 2c, prefix self-distillation therefore uses only final answers. Iterations 𝑘 𝑑/𝑐 receive cross-entropy on 𝑧𝑑. For each example, up to 𝑛𝑘 earlier iterations 𝑘 < 𝑑/𝑐 are trained to match, by KL divergence, the answer distribution of teacher that reads the same prompt truncated after 𝑐𝑘 steps, decoded at its own completion iteration. The teacher is an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student [31] or the live student.

(a) Architecture (3.1, 3.3): Retrofitted prelude 𝑃, weight-tied core 𝐶, and coda 𝑄, stabilized across iterations via RMS norm anchoring. (b) Progress alignment (3.2): Recurrent iteration 𝑘 predicts intermediate state 𝑧𝑘 after 𝑘 operations, establishing an explicit depthlength correspondence. (d) Learned halting (3.4): The coda jointly predicts task completion (Yes/No); inference terminates when multi-step confirmation window is met. at training or test time.

sections.title: 5.5 Prior benchmarks and scope
sections.content: Benchmarks from prior literature. Table 6 evaluates the recipes on the benchmark tasks on which the final-answer and unanchored recipes were introduced. On the rule-table chain, an inherently sequential lookup problem, PAR-hold reaches 𝐺 8 (94% accuracy at depth 64) and PAR reaches 6.0, whereas prefix targets without norm anchoring stall at 1.78. Inductive bias and task structure. Graph reachability is solved by expanding frontier in parallel rather than by fixed sequence of steps, so it has no canonical intermediate state for iteration 𝑘 to hold; all recipes stay below 3.5 on it. The correspondence targets sequential multi-step computation, the regime in which fixed-depth transformers fail [19, 21]. Natural-language format. On BIG-Bench-Hard-style [29] tracking shuffled objects format with natural-language swaps, trained on 16 swaps, PAR-hold with positional stretch reaches 9496% at 32 and 79% at 64 swaps (chance 17%), whereas random-𝑅 and fixed-depth baselines with the same stretch reach at most 67% and 21%. The original BBH items (3, 5 and 7 objects) lie within the training range, and all models score 95100% on them.

The correspondence needs stationary step map. Prefix targets without norm anchoring stall at 1.8 under either schedule, consistent with findings in unanchored recurrence [28], as state representations drift when iterated repeatedly. Together, the two conditions extrapolate at least 16. PAR reaches 𝐺 = 16 across all seeds with near-ceiling accuracy at 𝑑 = 256. sections.title:
6.2 Stopping rule and alternatives to halting
Stopping rule. Evaluating 𝑃(Yes) at a single iteration
is brittle (Table 8), as transient probability spikes cause
premature stopping at long horizons. Conversely, requiring
all 8 consecutive iterations to confirm completion is overly
strict when probabilities fluctuate, delaying stopping until
predictions drift. The “6 of 8” rule balances robustness and
responsiveness, matching oracle stopping within 1.6 points
across all evaluated sequences.

Training on extra iterations is not substitute. An alternative to an explicit halting signal is making completion an absorbing state by training models on extra iterations that must retain 𝑧𝑑. While this preserves in-distribution accuracy, it severely harms extrapolation: accuracy collapses below 1% at 16 across evaluated seeds. Asking the recurrent core to advance intermediate states while simultaneously acting as fixed point introduces conflicting objectives; an independent completion read-out avoids this competition.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: A looped language model extrapolates in depth when each of its iterations has defined job. Aligning iteration 𝑘 with the first 𝑘 steps of the problem, and keeping the step map stationary, turns extra iterations into extra reasoning. retrofitted 0.5B model trained this way surpasses the best published latent-recurrence model on swap-𝑆5 at 8 and 16 the training length. The same correspondence lets the model learn when to stop and lets it learn its intermediate states from final answers alone. Defining what an iteration means is thus training target in its own right, alongside choosing how many iterations to run.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We evaluate on algorithmic and templated state-tracking tasks, where intermediate states are well defined; applying the correspondence to open-ended natural-language reasoning [3638] is left to future work. Tasks without sequential decomposition, such as graph reachability, fall outside its scope. Our scaling study covers Qwen2.5 backbones up to 7B and Qwen3 backbones up to 4B, with three seeds each, in the single-query 𝑆5 setting only; swap-𝑆5, learned halting and prefix self-distillation are evaluated only on Qwen2.5-0.5B. On the larger backbones, as with prefix self-distillation, results vary across seeds far more than for PAR on Qwen2.5-0.5B (standard deviations of 3343 points at 16 on Qwen2.5-1.5B to 7B), accuracy does not rise monotonically with Qwen2.5 size, and no Qwen3 backbone approaches Qwen2.5-0.5B at 16. These results therefore do not establish monotonic trend with model size; characterizing the mechanisms of seed variance on larger backbones and stabilizing recurrent scaling remain open questions for future work.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work studies training methods on synthetic reasoning tasks with publicly available models [14, 40]. It involves no human subjects and no personal data. Latent reasoning writes no intermediate steps, which makes it less transparent than chain of thought. Under the correspondence, however, every iteration can be decoded into the intermediate answer it holds, which offers way to inspect the latent computation.
